data.title: Crypto Analyst Says Ethereum Is Retesting Multi-Year Resistance in Potential Breakout Setup, Targets $15,000 ETH
data.description:
Ethereum (ETH) may be en route to retesting a multi-year resistance zone for the third time after holding its long-term accumulation support.

Pseudonymous analyst Crypto Patel tells his 68,000 followers on X that Ethereum flashed a similar setup in 2020 before rallying to its cycle high close to $5,000.

“ETHEREUM BIGGEST BREAKOUT SETUP YET?

ETH is retesting a multi-year resistance zone for the 3rd time after holding its long-term accumulation support.

A breakout could open the path toward $5K – $10K – $15K.”

Looking at a potential catalyst for a strong Ethereum run, Fundstrat’s Tom Lee says he believes Ethereum “is the future settlement rails for Wall Street and AI.”

Lee also believes that Ethereum could spark a rally that will trigger sidelined investors to jump in.

“We think the asset with the most FOMO in Sept and into year-end will be crypto, particularly ETH.”

Meanwhile, another crypto analyst, Credible, believes that ETH could witness a slight correction below $2,500 before surging to $2,800.

“ETH has pulled back as expected, but I think there is a chance we may not yet be ready to take that downside liquidity just yet.

I like the idea of grinding higher and roping in some more longs before the eventual flush.

When we get these triple-tap bases, we will often pull back to the right ‘shoulder’ or local demand formed by the 3rd ‘tap’ before seeing continuation higher.

So while we’ve seen a deep pullback thus far, it is nothing that we can’t recover from if we are indeed going to continue a bit higher before the eventual flush.

On the upside, I have my eyes on the $2800+ region, which is local supply.”

data.title: Entrepreneur Accused of Posing as God in Texts to Defraud Investor of $60,000,000
data.description:
An entrepreneur is accused of impersonating divine messages through text messages to manipulate a devout elderly investor into funding a planned theme park rivaling Disney.

Richard M. Silanskas Jr. admitted in a deposition to sending text messages to 91-year-old O. Gene Bicknell labeled “Today’s Word” and signed as a nun named “Sister Catherine,” reports Inc.

The messages allegedly aimed to convince Bicknell that God commanded him to fund the American Heartland Theme Park in Vinita, Oklahoma, and grant Silanskas and partner Larry Wilhite two-thirds ownership of the $2 billion venture.

A 2025 complaint outlines Bicknell’s lawsuit against Silanskas and business partners Larry Wilhite and Stephen Hedrick, accusing the men of invoking religion to persuade him to hand over money for the theme-park project.

As stated in the court documents:

“Silanskas and Wilhite executed a predatory conspiracy of psychological manipulation—convincing Gene, through fraud and impersonation, that God himself was commanding him both to finance the park’s construction and to grant Silanskas and Wilhite two-thirds ownership over the completed venture, which was to be worth $2 billion.”

Silanskas used multiple email accounts while posing as a nun, but did not disclose that information during earlier hearings and only revealed it in June of this year.

Court documents further state:

“He made the ‘difficult decision’ to ‘tell the complete truth.’ By his own depiction, Silanskas decides for himself what information to withhold, when he feels comfortable revealing it, when he’ll lie, and when he’ll tell the truth.”

The project was canceled after minimal construction, and the suit includes RICO claims, civil conspiracy, fraud, deceit, and intentional infliction of emotional distress, mentioning Bicknell’s “crippling stroke in July 2024.”

data.title: Scammers Drain $20,000 From Texas Woman’s Wells Fargo Account: Report
data.description:
Scammers posing as Wells Fargo and FBI officials have drained $20,000 from a 75-year-old Texas woman through a phone scheme.

Police say callers convinced the victim to send the money to fix supposed problems with her bank account, reports Coconut Creek Talk.

She obtained a $20,000 cashier’s check and deposited it into a Wells Fargo account at a Kerrville, Texas branch.

An investigation led to the arrest of 23-year-old Ariana Theresa Johnson of Coconut Creek, Florida. She faces organized fraud against a person 65 or older, grand theft from a person 65 or older and money laundering charges.

Kerr County Sheriff’s investigators traced the receiving account to Johnson and another person who shared a Coconut Creek address and forwarded the case to Coconut Creek Police.

Johnson later confirmed she shared the Wells Fargo account with her mother and that the $20,000 entered the account on May 15th.

Bank records show the funds left through multiple electronic and in-person withdrawals in the days that followed.

Police arrested Johnson at her workplace on September 5th.

She allegedly admitted taking part in the scheme and claimed she acted at the request of a person known as Spizz.

Johnson did not identify that person and was booked into the Broward County Main Jail.

data.title: Morgan Stanley Strategist Mike Wilson Warning Of S&P 500 Correction Within 30 Days
data.description:
Rising oil prices are threatening to drain liquidity from markets and trigger a stock market correction within the next 30 days despite strong corporate earnings.

Morgan Stanley chief US equity strategist and chief investment officer Mike Wilson outlined the risk in a Bloomberg Television interview, reports The Street

Wilson pointed to potential oil prices of $120 to $140 a barrel as a major drain on available funds, combined with heavy corporate fundraising activity that could stretch investor capacity.

“I do think in the next 30 days, if oil goes to $120, $130, $140, that’s a drain on liquidity.”

U.S. benchmark WTI crude had risen 78.5% year-to-date through September 10, reaching $102.48 a barrel from $57.42 at the end of 2025.

Wilson noted that market valuations have adjusted and earnings growth continues to back indexes, keeping him overall bullish on stocks despite the short-term warning.

“But it’s a correction. It’s not the end of the world.”

Wilson said the correction could open up a window of opportunity for investors to accumulate high-quality names that efficiently generate free cash flow.

“We’re rotating as opposed to reducing our overall equity exposure. I don’t think people should be reducing their equity exposure.”

The Morgan Stanley strategist adds that the S&P 500 remains his top choice over foreign indexes.

“S&P 500 is still the highest quality equity market in the world.”

As of Friday’s close, the S&P 500 is trading at 7,656.

data.title: Woman Loses $73,000 After Bank of America Fraud-Unit Impersonators Direct Massive Wire Transfer: Report
data.description:
A Georgia woman has reportedly lost $73,000 after callers posing as Bank of America fraud investigators and a police sergeant pushed her to pool her savings and wire the money out.

A woman claiming to work in the bank’s fraud unit said someone was stealing from her and patched her through to a supposed officer who had her move everything into one account, reports Mainstreet News.

The callers then told her to go to a Bank of America branch and send a wire to stop the theft.

At a branch, staff warned her she was being scammed. The caller then told her to leave and invent a different story at the next location.

She completed the $73,000 wire at a different Bank of America branch.

After she got home and told her husband, he knew she had been scammed. She called the bank to try to stop the transfer and later learned the money was already gone.

Banks typically treat wires that customers send in person as authorized transfers, which means the money is hard to get back and reimbursement rarely happens.

data.title: Elderly Woman From Massachusetts Masterminds $10,930,940 Ponzi Scheme Impacting 204 Victims
data.description:
Investors in Massachusetts have lost nearly $11 million after a promissory-note Ponzi scheme drained a West Springfield loan business.

Barbara A. Hirshfield, 83, of Lexington, has pleaded guilty to five counts of wire fraud for running a Ponzi scheme through Ideal Financial Services Inc. and Ideal Financial Holdings, says the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Massachusetts.

Prosecutors say she sold notes promising high fixed returns and told buyers the cash would fund motor vehicle and small loans, with interest paid from borrower repayments.

State regulators flagged Ideal’s finances in 2012 and later stripped its licenses to issue those loans, cutting off its main revenue.

Hirshfield kept raising outside money anyway and used fresh investments to cover interest and principal owed to earlier noteholders, blaming banking issues, fraud, data breaches and lost checks when payments slipped.

“It is alleged that Hirshfield used money obtained from new investments to make interest and principal payments owed to earlier investors, operating Ideal as a Ponzi scheme.”

The scheme collapsed around June of 2025, leaving 204 victims with losses of $10,930,940, and more than 25 faced substantial financial hardship.

One longtime investor, Kimberly O’Connor, says her family’s stake stretched back generations and included everything she inherited from her mother.

“It was a lot of excuses at that point… And that’s when we started really trying to pull out money.”

Wire fraud carries up to 20 years in prison, three years of supervised release and a $250,000 fine.

data.title: Washington State Women Orchestrate Identity Theft and Bank Fraud Operation, Hitting Over 250 People
data.description:
A pair of Washington women have admitted to running an identity theft and bank fraud operation that hit more than 250 victims over multiple years.

The DOJ says Emily Vranic, 34, and Heather Marquis, 37, of Bremerton used stolen mail to activate fraudulent credit cards, open new accounts and seize control of existing bank accounts.

One victim faced $110,000 in unauthorized transfers that could have climbed past $170,000 without bank intervention.

Prosecutors say the pair repeatedly rerouted mail through third-party addresses and even used victim funds to cover their own mortgage payments.

Vranic drew a three-year prison term while Marquis received 31 months, followed by three years of supervised release for each.

Says First Assistant U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd,

“These defendants attempted to steal at least $330,000 from their victims over a three-year period – ID theft and bank fraud was their ‘job,’ and for at least 15 victims they were all too successful.”

Marquis agreed to pay $102,784 in restitution while Vranic’s restitution hearing remains scheduled for October of 2026.

Investigators say the pair also stole private records including tax documents, Social Security cards and military papers.

data.title: Alleged Scammer Drains $33,000+ From Connecticut Bank in Forgery and Identity Theft Scheme
data.description:
A Connecticut bank has lost more than $33,000 after police say forged paperwork, stolen identities and impersonation powered a string of fraudulent withdrawals.

Bryan David Sheriff, 25, of West Morningside St. in Hartford, is facing multiple felony counts in the case, reports WFSB.

Thomaston Savings Bank’s fraud department alerted Thomaston police to the suspected fraud on June 18th, 2026.

Detectives then worked the case with the bank, Watertown police, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and the U.S. Treasury Department.

Police say the probe uncovers an elaborate scam built around forgeries, identity theft and impersonation. According to authorities, detectives “unraveled an elaborate scam involving various forgeries, identity thefts and impersonations resulting in fraudulent bank withdrawals totaling more than $33,000.”

Sheriff faces charges of first-degree larceny, conspiracy to commit first-degree larceny, trafficking personal identifying information, first-degree identity theft, first-degree forgery and false statement to procure issuance of a payment card.

Sheriff, who has prior convictions for gun and drug offenses as well as conspiracy to commit robbery, was being held Friday at MacDougall-Walker Correctional Institution on a $250,000 bond.

Police say an arrest warrant remains outstanding for an alleged co-conspirator.

Thomaston Savings Bank is a community bank based in Connecticut with $1.9 billion in total assets.

data.title: Ex-Pastor and Bank Vice-President Scams Individuals and Institutions out of at Least $9,395,882 in Alleged ‘Cattle-Buying’ Scheme
data.description:
A former Missouri bank vice president and pastor is pleading guilty to federal fraud charges after running a cattle investment scheme that defrauded victims and his employer of millions.

The 45-year-old Butler resident worked as a vice president and loan officer at Community First Bank while serving as a pastor, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Missouri.

From at least April 2024 until his termination in February 2026, he solicited funds for buying and quickly selling cattle but instead placed the money in an investment account.

“Johnson did not use the funds to purchase cattle but instead deposited the funds in an investment account where he repeatedly traded in small-capitalization and micro-cap securities ultimately losing all the funds.”

Johnson served as loan officer for about 29 loans and lines of credit totaling roughly $4.48 million at the bank, creating some without victims’ knowledge or approval, including at least three in February 2026 to pay off earlier fraudulent loans.

Prosecutors described how he operated.

“Johnson used his position at Community First Bank to obtain loans using the identity of other people. At various times between April 2024 and until Johnson’s termination in February 2026, Johnson used his position as a loan officer and/or his status in the community to defraud individuals and a financial institution of at least $9,395,882.22.”

He used some victim funds to pay prior investors to conceal the scheme.

A sentencing hearing is pending after a pre-sentence investigation.

data.title: New Jersey Duo Steal $670,313 Worth of Checks From USPS Collection Boxes
data.description:
Two New Jersey men are admitting their roles in a conspiracy to steal checks from the mail and engaging in check washing in order to cash out.

The operation targeted USPS collection boxes in Livingston and Clifton using stolen postal keys and caused financial institutions to lose $670,313.46, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office, District of New Jersey

Leslie Blackwood, 25, of Irvington, entered his guilty plea in Newark federal court on Wednesday to conspiracy to steal checks from the mail.

His accomplice, Verly Antenor, 24, of Roselle Park, had previously pleaded guilty to the same charge.

According to the prosecution, stolen or misappropriated keys to gain access to USPS’ collection boxes.

“To profit from the scheme, Blackwood and Antenor sold, deposited, or caused to be deposited the stolen checks to fraudulently obtain funds from financial institutions. Blackwood and Antenor sometimes “washed” the stolen checks by erasing the date, payee, amount, and memo line from the stolen checks and replacing the information, oftentimes for higher amounts than the amounts originally written on the checks.”

The men worked with others from 2021 to 2022, depositing the checks at various banks and sometimes washing them to raise the amounts.

Antenor is scheduled for sentencing on Dec. 17 while Blackwood will be sentenced on Feb. 16, 2027. The charges stemming from the conspiracy to commit mail theft could see each of the two individuals facing up to
five years in prison and a fine of up to a quarter of a million dollars.
